text:
I’m starting to think watching benchmarks is creating upgrade problems I didn’t actually have

I was perfectly happy with my PC last week..but well.   
I have a 5800X3D, a 4070 Ti, 32GB of RAM, and I play at 1440p. Nothing I play feels bad. Cyberpunk runs well. Baldur’s Gate 3 runs well. Helldivers 2 runs well. I can pick basically anything random from my Steam library and have a good time.   
Then I made the mistake of watching GPU benchmarks.  
Suddenly I’m staring at charts where my perfectly good card gets 105 FPS and some newer card gets 145, and my brain immediately decides that missing 40 FPS is now a problem I need to fix.  
Two hours earlier I didn’t even know I was “missing” anything.  
Then comes the usual spiral. Check used prices for my current GPU. Open PCPartPicker. Start telling myself I could sell this, add a few hundred, upgrade that, maybe finally move to AM5 while I’m at it...And suddenly I’ve mentally spent $1,500 fixing a PC I was happily gaming on that same morning. Well I tested this on myself yesterday. Turned the FPS counter off completely and played for about three hours. I genuinely could not tell you if I was getting 90 FPS, 110, or 140 most of the time.   
The game just felt good. Then I turned the counter back on and immediately started noticing every dip again.  
I’m starting to think benchmarks are extremely useful when you actually need to buy something, but kind of dangerous when you don’t. There’s always another graph showing that your hardware is 20% or 30% behind something newer, and once you see that number it’s weirdly hard to stop thinking about it.   
Obviously some upgrades make a massive difference. Going from 60Hz to high refresh, HDD to SSD, or from struggling on low settings to comfortably running high settings. You notice those immediately. But I think I’ve reached the point where the main thing making my PC feel “old” is YouTube showing me how much faster somebody else’s is.  
Probably time to stop benchmarking the damn thing and just play games on it.  
Obviously there are real upgrades that make a huge difference. Going from 60Hz to high refresh, HDD to SSD, struggling at low settings to comfortably running high settings, those are obvious.  
But I think I’ve reached the point where the biggest thing making my PC feel “old” is YouTube telling me how much faster somebody else’s is.  
Might be time to stop benchmarking my computer and actually use the damn thing

text:
My PC has parts from so many different upgrade eras that I’m not sure I even have a “build” anymore

I was looking at my parts list the other day and realized basically nothing in this PC belongs to the same generation.  
The case is from my first proper build. PSU is a few years newer. Storage has been replaced and added to multiple times. GPU is relatively recent. CPU and motherboard are somewhere in the middle. RAM was upgraded later because 16GB started feeling cramped. Even the fans have been swapped at different points because some died and some were just annoying.  
Well, PC still works completely fine. There’s no single component I can point at and say “this is obviously the problem.” But trying to plan the next upgrade is getting weird because every change seems to expose something else.  
If I upgrade the GPU, I start thinking about whether the PSU is old enough that I should replace it too. If I upgrade the CPU, that probably means a new motherboard and RAM. Then I look at the case and think maybe I should finally get something with better airflow. At that point I’m basically building a new PC anyway, except I still have three perfectly usable SSDs and maybe a cooler I can reuse.  
I always thought upgrading over time was supposed to make PC ownership cheaper and easier. Instead I’ve somehow created this Ship of Theseus situation where the machine has been replaced piece by piece and now I have no idea which upgrade actually makes sense next.  
Part of me wants to keep stretching it because there’s something satisfying about a PC surviving this many generations. The other part is starting to think there’s a point where incremental upgrades stop being clever and you should just admit the “same PC” argument has gotten a little way to serious

text:
My 6-year-old PC still does everything I need, and somehow that makes upgrading harder

I’ve been “about to build a new PC” for probably a year now.  
Current system is a Ryzen 5 3600, RTX 2070 Super, 16GB DDR4 and a couple of SSDs. I built it in 2020 and at the time I assumed I’d get maybe 4-5 years out of it before something started feeling painfully outdated.  
Well... apparently nobody told the PC.  
I play at 1440p. Most of what I actually play is stuff like Baldur’s Gate 3, Helldivers 2, older RPGs, strategy games and whatever random indie game steals two weeks of my life. I’ve had to turn settings down in newer games, obviously. I’m not pretending a 2070 Super is secretly a 5080. But I launch a game, change a couple settings, and then... it works.  
And that’s the problem.  
Every few months I get the upgrade itch. I watch benchmarks, build a parts list, convince myself that this is finally the year. New CPU would be nice. 32GB would be nice. A modern GPU would be REALLY nice. Then I look at the total, go play something on my current PC, and within five minutes I’m thinking “wait, what exactly am I trying to fix?”  
Well...kinda funny that I can afford a new build now much more comfortably than I could when I built this one. I actually want to build one. Half the fun for me is picking parts and putting the thing together.  
But spending a few thousand dollars just to turn settings from “high” to “ultra” and watch an FPS counter become a bigger number feels harder to justify than I expected.  
I always thought upgrading would happen because my old PC became unusable. Instead it’s slowly turning into this weird negotiation where the old bastard keeps doing just enough to survive another generation.  
I’ve even caught myself almost rooting for something to finally struggle badly enough that I can upgrade without feeling stupid about it.  
For now I keep closing PCPartPicker tabs and telling myself “maybe next generation,” which is exactly what I said last generation

text:
First build sleep crashing

I have been using chat bot to help me log and keep things organized. Below is a summary of my last week fighting with my first build and then giving up and handing it to Micro Center. I had another post that was a mess that I to make this summary of events.

#  PC keeps crashing/rebooting during automatic sleep — Micro Center troubleshooting

I wanted to provide an update on my troubleshooting since my last Reddit post. This has turned into a longer process than I expected, and I’m still trying to determine whether the original problem has actually been resolved.

# My PC specs

* **CPU:** Intel Core Ultra 7 270K Plus
* **CPU cooler:** Thermalright Peerless Assassin 120 SE
* **Motherboard:** Gigabyte Z890 EAGLE WIFI7 PLUS
* **RAM:** G.Skill 32GB (2×16GB) DDR5-6000 CL36
* **SSD:** Crucial P510 1TB PCIe Gen 5 NVMe
* **GPU originally installed:** ASRock Challenger OC Radeon RX 9060 XT 16GB
* **Replacement GPU:** ASUS Radeon RX 9060 XT Dual Fan 16GB
* **PSU:** MSI MAG A750GL PCIE5 750W 80+ Gold
* **OS:** Windows 11 Home

# Original problem

My PC would unexpectedly crash and reboot when left idle. The problem seemed related to the display turning off and Windows entering automatic sleep.

I observed two behaviors:

1. With the display timeout set to one minute and system sleep set to **Never**, the PC would sometimes reboot roughly five minutes after the display turned off.
2. When system sleep was enabled, the PC would sometimes crash/reboot when Windows attempted to enter sleep automatically.

Manually selecting Sleep from the Start menu had previously worked normally. The problem was intermittent, which made it difficult to determine whether a change had actually fixed it.

# Troubleshooting before Micro Center

I updated Windows, installed motherboard-related updates through Gigabyte Control Center, checked the BIOS, and performed a clean AMD graphics driver installation using AMD Cleanup Utility and Adrenalin.

I also reseated the GPU, disabled PCIe Link State Power Management, and tried different power settings.

Some tests seemed to point toward the discrete GPU or its connection:

* The problem occurred using both my monitor and a TV connected to the GPU's HDMI port.
* Connecting the TV to the motherboard's DisplayPort using a DP-to-HDMI adapter, while leaving the GPU installed, appeared stable during testing.
* Removing the GPU and using the CPU's integrated graphics was stable during display-timeout testing.
* With the GPU removed, automatic sleep and waking back up also worked during the test I performed.

I also had repeated **LiveKernelEvent 193** graphics watchdog reports. The associated dump information referenced Windows graphics components such as `dxgkrnl.sys`, `dxgmms2.sys`, and `watchdog.sys`, as well as AMD's `amdkmdag.sys`.

These results made the graphics path suspicious, but they did not conclusively identify whether the GPU, driver, PCIe connection, firmware, power delivery, or another interaction was responsible.

# What Micro Center found

Micro Center tested my original ASRock GPU on a separate test bench, where it passed their testing with different software.

However, when they tested that same GPU in my PC using OCCT's 3D Adaptive test, it failed with a GPU core error and thousands of logged errors.

The original GPU was replaced under warranty with an ASUS RX 9060 XT 16GB.

Unfortunately, the replacement GPU also initially failed OCCT testing in my PC. This time, the report looked more like a general system crash rather than the original card's GPU core failure.

The technicians told me that the PSU and PCIe slot had passed preliminary tests. They also later confirmed that a known-good GPU had been tested in my system and passed testing. I don't know whether that test included the exact same automatic sleep/display-timeout scenarios that caused my original problem.

# More recent Micro Center updates

A technician reported that a clean graphics driver installation had resolved the graphics crashing during testing. My understanding was that the previous technician had used DDU to wipe the existing graphics drivers and then installed them fresh with the replacement GPU.

However, the PC reportedly crashed once during testing even after that clean installation. Later, the technician said it had not crashed again when the display turned off and that it was staying on with the sleep settings enabled.

I specifically asked them to verify both original behaviors:

* Whether the PC still rebooted roughly five minutes after the display turned off with system sleep set to Never.
* Whether it could reliably enter automatic sleep and wake back up without crashing.

The technician said the PC had not crashed with the sleep settings and that the display-off behavior was stable, so they planned to proceed with the tune-up.

Then I received another update saying the previous technician was still having issues with the sleep/wake cycle and had suggested updating the BIOS to see if that resolved the remaining issue.

That left me uncertain about the actual status. It wasn't clear from the updates whether the BIOS had already been updated, whether the sleep issue had subsequently passed repeated testing, or whether the latest stable results were simply short tests.

The technicians rotate from day to day, so the person giving me an update may not be the same person who performed the previous tests.

# Where things stand

I've sent a message explaining that my main concern is the original sleep-related crash. I've also explained that Micro Center is more than an hour away, so repeated trips to pick up the PC and bring it back if the problem returns would be difficult.

I asked them to confirm that the original issue was specifically tested after any BIOS update or other changes, that the PC remained stable through repeated display-timeout and automatic sleep/wake tests, what they believe ultimately resolved the issue, and how long it had been tested without another crash.

I'm not expecting a guarantee that the computer will never crash again. I just want reasonable confidence that the original problem has been addressed before I drive out to collect it.

**My main question:** Given that both GPUs initially failed OCCT testing in my system, the original card passed testing on a separate bench, a known-good GPU reportedly passed in my PC, and a clean graphics driver installation appeared to help, what would you consider the most likely explanation? Also, what specific testing would you want to see before considering this issue resolved?

I'm trying to avoid jumping to conclusions. I want to understand whether this was primarily a graphics driver/software issue, a BIOS or power-management issue, a hardware interaction, or something else.
label: Troubleshooting

**Specs**

* MSI RTX 5070 12G Gaming Trio OC, bought new in July. VBIOS 98.05.4A.00.09
* Ryzen 9 5900X (no iGPU)
* ASRock B550M PG Riptide, BIOS L3.62

It started in July (shrtly after purchase) in games (Darktide, Vermintide 2, Total War), then in Unity, and now it happens on the desktop doing nothing, but very randomly and during start of most random tasks. * PCIe Link State Power Management off
* Reseated the card, support bracket under it, cable fully clicked in
